standard.title: Analyse and visualise data
standard.description: analyse and visualise data interactively using a range of software, including spreadsheets and databases, to draw conclusions and make predictions by identifying trends and outliers
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse and visualise data using a range of software including spreadsheets and databases (AC9TDI8P02). They can identify trends and patterns in data and draw conclusions from visualisations. They have not yet developed interactive visualisations, applied machine learning as a form of analysis, or adjusted model parameters to observe effects on predictions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse and visualise data interactively using spreadsheets and databases to draw conclusions and make predictions by identifying trends and outliers, including developing interactive visualisations and exploring how machine learning models analyse patterns in data.

nodes.label: Summarising data and identifying trends
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can summarise a dataset by identifying its attributes, relationships between variables, trends and outliers.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a dataset, identify at least one trend and one outlier; describe what each indicates about the data.
nodes.typical_width: Summarise a dataset's attributes and the relationships between variables; identify multiple trends and outliers; explain what each finding suggests and whether outliers are errors or genuinely interesting data points.
wider: Summarise electoral data including demographics, historical swings and exceptions — identify what trends predict outcomes and where exceptions undermine simple predictions
Investigate why the same dataset can show different trends depending on how it is grouped or filtered — connecting this to statistical concepts of aggregation

response_modes.reason: Trend and outlier identification requires systematic data reading — students who scan data intuitively often miss outliers or misread trend direction. Scaffolding the analysis (describe the range → identify central tendency → find exceptions → name the direction) produces reliable summary before prediction.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one trend in a dataset and describes its direction
Identifies at least one outlier and explains whether it represents an error or a genuine data point
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify trends and outliers in a dataset cannot draw conclusions or make predictions at N2 — the N2 checkpoint is directly dependent on the data summary produced at N1.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions and making predictions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions from data analysis and make predictions, including identifying the limits of the prediction.
nodes.minimum_width: Draw at least one conclusion from a dataset and make one prediction; note one limitation of the prediction.
nodes.typical_width: Draw multiple conclusions from a dataset with different variables; make predictions by extending observed trends; identify what would need to be true for the predictions to hold and where they might fail.
wider: Investigate emerging trends in Australia's industries using ABS data — make predictions about future employment patterns and identify what assumptions underpin each prediction
Analyse historical data to predict a future outcome (election, environmental trend, economic indicator) and explain what factors could cause the prediction to be wrong

response_modes.reason: Students often confuse correlation with causation when making predictions, or state predictions without identifying their limiting assumptions. A reasoning scaffold — what does the trend show? → what would have to be true for this to continue? → what could break this pattern? — builds rigour in prediction-making.

success_criteria: States a conclusion that is grounded in the data (not just restating the data)
Makes a prediction and identifies at least one assumption or limitation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify limiting assumptions for predictions cannot meaningfully design interactive visualisations at N3 — the analytical intent of the visualisation depends on knowing what question is being asked and what its limitations are.

nodes.label: Developing interactive visualisations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop interactive visualisations for exploring complex data, allowing users to control and view different aspects of a dataset.
nodes.minimum_width: Create a visualisation with at least one interactive element (e.g. a filter, slider, or chart type selector) that allows a user to change what is displayed.
nodes.typical_width: Develop an interactive visualisation for a complex dataset — include multiple views or filters that allow exploration of relationships, trends and outliers; explain how the interactive design helps users explore the data.
wider: Develop a motion chart or time-series interactive visualisation (e.g. population, life expectancy and fertility rate) that allows users to explore change over time
Design an interactive dashboard with linked views where selecting a data point in one chart filters or highlights related data in another
Incorporate sliders to allow users to adjust visualisation parameters and observe the effect on how patterns appear

response_modes.reason: Interactive visualisation requires coordinating data analysis, visual design and interactivity implementation. Students who understand each individually often struggle to build a visualisation that is both analytically useful and usable. The integration node is where analysis intent, visual form and interaction mechanism must work together.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Motion charts, linked views and time-series sliders are genuinely rich directions — each requires students to think about what question the visualisation is answering and how interaction helps users explore it. This is substantive UX-meets-data work.
success_criteria: Visualisation includes at least one interactive element that changes what is displayed
The interaction serves an analytical purpose — it helps the user explore the data, not just decorative

nodes.label: Machine learning as a form of data analysis
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how machine learning trains algorithms on data to identify patterns and classify inputs, and explore how adjusting model parameters affects outputs.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe what machine learning is and explain, using one example, how an algorithm is trained on data to classify new inputs.
nodes.typical_width: Use a machine learning tool to train a model on a dataset and classify new inputs; adjust at least one parameter and observe how it changes the model's output; explain what the parameter controls.
wider: Explore how adjusting the weighting of different input variables in a model changes its predictions — explain what this reveals about which variables have most influence
Investigate how training data composition affects model output — what happens when certain categories are underrepresented? Connect this to real-world bias in deployed AI systems
Use a visual ML tool (e.g. Teachable Machine) to train image classifiers and observe how classification accuracy changes as training data volume increases

response_modes.reason: Machine learning is conceptually opaque — students often treat it as a black box. Multiple hands-on experiments (image classification, parameter adjustment, training data variation) each make a different aspect of the process visible, building a more complete mental model than a single experiment.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Training data bias and parameter effects are both conceptually rich and consequential directions — they connect directly to real-world AI ethics and decision-making quality in deployed systems.
success_criteria: Correctly explains that ML algorithms learn patterns from training data
Demonstrates that changing training data or parameters changes model output
Can explain in plain language what changed and why
